takeaway: PreAcher lets a CDN reject most bad password logins through privacy-preserving pre-authentication, while a trusted origin server retains the final password check.
background: Slow password hashes defend stored credentials against guessing but make login endpoints computationally expensive. CDNs can absorb attacks, yet conventional HTTPS termination exposes passwords to them.
villain: Existing defenses do not simultaneously keep failed-login computation away from the origin, hide passwords from the CDN, and preserve ordinary browser login behavior.
approach: During registration, the client and trusted origin create an encrypted pre-authentication key record that the origin places at the CDN. At login, browser-delivered JavaScript uses username-keyed locality-sensitive hashing plus an oblivious pseudorandom function to recover the signing key associated with a similarity bucket; the CDN verifies its signature without learning the exact password. Only then does the CDN forward the password, encrypted to the origin's public key, for a conventional slow-hash check.
impact: The authors argue that a website can deploy this split check using CDN serverless code and page JavaScript to withstand login ADoS without changing browsers or CDN infrastructure.

evaluation.overview: The authors combine formal protocol analysis with prototype measurements of attack resilience, authentication throughput, CPU time, and Internet login latency.
evaluation.implemented: A JavaScript client library and CDN serverless function plus a C++ origin server using Sogou Workflow and standard cryptographic libraries.
evaluation.setting: A three-VM Azure testbed with 4 vCPUs and 8 GiB per VM, plus a Cloudflare Internet deployment with Azure clients and origin; PBKDF2 is the full-authentication hash.
baselines: Baseline: CDN forwards every login to the origin
SGX-CDN: password authentication inside Intel SGX via Occlum

results.text: The authors report that, in the testbed ADoS experiment, 100 valid requests/s competed with 400 invalid requests/s; PreAcher served 97 successful logins/s, whereas the other methods served nearly none.
The authors report that, on the testbed, PreAcher's failed-login pre-authentication handled 948 requests/s at 23% CPU, versus 99 and 91 requests/s at 100% CPU for DuoHash and SGX-CDN.

limitations: The security argument assumes an honest-but-curious CDN that follows the protocol, a trusted origin and client platform, and an ADoS-resistant registration path; active CDN attackers are left for future work. PreAcher protects passwords and login authentication, not other application-layer attack surfaces, post-login cookies, general private traffic, password reuse, or origin compromise.
phd_group_signal: This work reflects a security-systems methodology that combines protocol construction and proof with deployable web components, adversarial analysis, and end-to-end performance experiments.

claims.text: PreAcher combines username-keyed weighted K-mer MinHash with an OPRF-derived envelope key so a client can prove membership in a password-similarity bucket to the CDN, after which the origin performs the exact password check.

The paper assumes a passive CDN, a trusted origin and client platform, and ADoS-resistant registration; it excludes active CDN behavior, origin compromise, non-login ADoS surfaces, general private traffic, and post-login cookie protection.

The prototype places client operations in page-delivered JavaScript and CDN operations in serverless edge code, so deployment changes the website's login page and origin processing but not browser or CDN infrastructure.
